title: Money rules
summary: One simple rule removes all awkwardness and suspicion: the companion never handles the elder's cash.

lessons.title: Why money needs a strict rule
lessons.body:
Elders behave very differently around money:

- **Kanjoos:** questions every rupee.
- **Shakki:** “tumne zyada toh nahi diya?”, suspects they're being cheated.
- **Carefree:** happily spends, can be overcharged.
- **Guilt or pride:** wants to pay themselves so their child isn't burdened.

One rule protects you from all four: **you never take, hold or pay the elder's cash.**

lessons.title: The rules
lessons.body:
1. **Never handle the elder's cash.** The elder pays directly (cash, card or UPI at the counter), or the child pays remotely.
2. **Never pay from your own pocket,** even if they say “paise baad mein de dunga”.
3. **Photo of every bill and receipt.** It goes into the report to the child.
4. **No tips, cash gifts or loans.** Politely refuse: “Uncle, PeakAge ka rule hai, main nahi le sakta. Aapka pyaar hi kaafi hai.”
5. **Never borrow money** or share your own UPI for an elder's payment.

> Taking cash from an elder means **immediate removal** from the platform, no second chance.

lessons.title: Tricky situations
lessons.body:
| Situation | What you do |
| --- | --- |
| Uncle hands you ₹2,000 to pay at the pharmacy | Walk with him to the counter so he pays himself |
| Elder can't walk to the counter | Call the child; they can pay by UPI to the hospital or pharmacy, or tell you how to proceed |
| Aunty insists you take ₹500 for your time | Refuse politely, every time, with a smile |
| Pharmacy has no card machine and elder has no cash | Call the child and the coordinator. Don't pay yourself. |
| Elder suspects the bill is too high | Show the bill, compare it with the prescription together |

questions.text: Uncle hands you his wallet and says “aap hi pay kar do”. What do you do?
options: Walk with him to the counter so he pays himself
Pay with your own UPI and take cash later
questions.explanation: Never handle the elder's cash. Help them pay directly.

questions.text: Aunty insists you keep ₹500 for being so helpful. What do you do?
questions.explanation: No tips or cash gifts. Refuse politely, every time.

questions.text: The elder has no cash and the pharmacy has no card machine. What do you do?
options: Call the child and the coordinator
questions.explanation: Never pay yourself. The child or coordinator decides how to proceed.

questions.text: What must you do with every bill and receipt?
options: Take a photo for the report to the child
questions.explanation: A photo of every bill goes into the report. It removes suspicion.

questions.text: What is the consequence of taking cash from an elder?
questions.explanation: Taking cash is zero-tolerance: immediate removal.

questions.text: Uncle says, “Abhi aap de do, paise baad mein de dunga.” What do you say?
options: Politely refuse and help him pay directly or call the child
Ask the pharmacist to give credit
questions.explanation: Never pay from your own pocket, even if they promise to pay later.

questions.text: A suspicious uncle thinks the bill is too high. What's the best way to handle it?
options: Show the bill and compare it with the prescription together
questions.explanation: Transparency removes suspicion. Check it together.
